run.question:
Alertmanager alert RequestErrorRate (severity warning) is firing for service otel-demo/frontend-proxy since 2026-11-15T12:50:59Z.
Investigate why this alert is firing.

report.summary: The RequestErrorRate warning for otel-demo/frontend-proxy is being driven by a small, ongoing stream of Envoy-generated 503 responses on the proxy's server spans (operation "ingress"). The proxy's own access log states the exact failure mode: response code 503 with flag UC and detail upstream_reset_before_response_started{connection_termination}, with the upstream endpoint identified as the frontend pod IP 100.96.4.190:8080 — i.e. the frontend backend closed the upstream connection before response headers were sent. The matching traces contain a frontend-proxy ingress span with http.status_code=503 plus a child "router frontend egress" span with error="true" and http.status_code="0" (no response), and no frontend server span for the failed request; the load-generator's own client spans for those requests return 503. The frontend service itself records no ERROR spans at all during the window and its pod/deployment are Running/Ready with 0 restarts, and the proxy pod is likewise healthy; the frontend does show CPU throttling (34.5% of CFS periods, 100m limit) and a small, slow memory rise (123–128 MiB of 200Mi), which is a candidate contributor but does not on its own explain a connection termination rather than a timeout. Why the frontend terminates these reused upstream connections (e.g. Node/Next.js keep-alive idle-socket close racing with Envoy connection reuse vs. health-check/connection-drain behaviour) is not resolved by the available evidence, so the conclusion is partial. Volume is low: frontend-proxy ingress error spans were 1.28–8.42 per 10 minutes (peak 8.42 at 12:54:59, 6.32 at the 12:50:59 alert anchor), i.e. ~0.03%–0.12% of frontend-proxy spans, all on the "ingress" operation; the egress operation has zero errors.

claims.text: frontend-proxy span metrics contain ERROR status only for the server operation "ingress": sum by span_name,status_code of increase(traces_span_metrics_calls_total{service_name="frontend-proxy"}[10m]) is 1.278 at 12:28:59, 3.251 at 12:34:59, 6.316 at 12:50:59 (the alert anchor), peaks at 8.421 at 12:54:59 and is 2.091 at 13:06:59, while "router frontend egress" has 0 errors at every step; ingress UNSET spans run ~7,150–7,300 per 10 minutes.

The frontend-proxy error fraction computed as error spans / all frontend-proxy spans per 10 minutes is 0.00029–0.00116 for span_name "ingress" (maximum 0.00116 at 12:54:59) and 0 for "router frontend egress" over 12:27:59–13:06:59.

In the frontend-proxy pod's Envoy access log, every failing request between 12:26:16.225 and 12:45:08.712 is logged as 503 with response flag UC and detail "upstream_reset_before_response_started{connection_termination}", 95 response bytes, upstream host "frontend 100.96.4.190:<port>" on port 8080, and request durations of 51 ms to 800 ms; all 8 such lines in that period have the identical flag/detail, e.g. "GET / HTTP/1.1" 503 UC ... 767 ms at 12:44:20.281 and "GET /api/products/1YMWWN1N4O" 503 UC ... 389 ms at 12:45:08.712.

The trace sample for 12:20:00–13:08:49 contains 8 frontend-proxy "ingress" spans with status error=true, http.status_code=503, otel.status_code=ERROR, each with a CHILD_OF "router frontend egress" span of the same service carrying error="true" and http.status_code="0" (no upstream response); the matching load-generator client spans (operation GET, under user_browse_product, user_index, user_add_to_cart, user_get_ads, user_get_recommendations) also carry error=true and http.status_code=503, and the failing traces contain no frontend server span for the failed request (e.g. trace_id 006109e39dbc3e0e38ea35e8110e2b5c, 18abc47459b7bc819f3193d49f6fadef, 57250c0c8c15f32c8f07fb3d10fd5833).

The frontend service records no ERROR spans of its own in the window: sum by span_name,status_code of increase(traces_span_metrics_calls_total{service_name="frontend"}[10m]) is 0 for STATUS_CODE_ERROR on every operation (GET, POST, the /api route operations, grpc.oteldemo.AdService/GetAds, CartService/AddItem, CartService/GetCart, CheckoutService/PlaceOrder, ProductCatalogService/GetProduct, RecommendationService/ListRecommendations, tcp.connect, dns.lookup), while its spans are recorded as STATUS_CODE_UNSET (not a success code).

Across services, error span increase per 10 minutes at 13:06:59 is 2.09 for frontend-proxy, 1.05 for ad, 1.04–2.12 for fraud-detection and 1.05 for recommendation, and exactly 0 for accounting, checkout, frontend and payment.

The ad, fraud-detection and recommendation error spans are on flagd event-stream client operations, not on request path operations: ad and fraud-detection record them on span_name "flagd.evaluation.v1.Service/EventStream" and recommendation on "/flagd.evaluation.v1.Service/EventStream", while the corresponding ResolveBoolean/ResolveInt spans have 0 errors.

Kubernetes state shows frontend pod frontend-675fd7b5c5-ssc7t (owner frontend-675fd7b5c5) Running and ready with restart count 0, started 2026-11-15T12:12:01Z, and frontend-proxy pod frontend-proxy-6b4d584985-bf4lq (owner frontend-proxy-6b4d584985) Running and ready with restart count 0, started 2026-11-15T12:12:03Z; their deployments report desired/available/ready = 1/1/1.

Resource configuration and use: the frontend container has CPU limit 100m and memory limit 200Mi (requests 50m/100Mi), and the frontend-proxy container has CPU limit 30m and memory limit 50Mi (requests 15m/25Mi).

Over the 10 minutes ending 13:06:00 the frontend container was throttled in 0.345 (34.5%) of CFS periods and the frontend-proxy container in 0.070 (7.0%); average CPU over that window was ~0.052 cores for frontend (of the 0.1 core limit) and ~0.014 cores for frontend-proxy (of the 0.03 core limit).

Container memory working set for frontend rises only slowly, from 123,199,488 bytes (12:30:00) to 128,442,368 bytes (13:05:00) against the 200Mi limit, and frontend-proxy stays at ~20.2 MB against its 50Mi limit; the frontend V8 old_space used bytes oscillate 34.9–45.2 MB against an old_space limit of ~50.9 MB, i.e. heap is heavily recycled rather than monotonically leaking.

The flagd ConfigMap read at 13:10:22 lists every fault-injection flag (adFailure, adHighCpu, adManualGc, cartFailure, emailMemoryLeak, imageSlowLoad, kafkaQueueProblems, loadGeneratorFloodHomepage, paymentFailure, paymentUnreachable, productCatalogFailure, recommendationCacheFailure) with defaultVariant "off"; this is configuration at query time, not incident-time runtime flag state.

Most likely mechanism for the 503 UC stream: the frontend's HTTP server (Node.js/Next.js) was closing idle upstream keep-alive sockets while Envoy still held them in its upstream connection pool and reused one, so the in-flight request hit a terminating connection and Envoy emitted its local 503. This fits the observed signature (sporadic single/double 503s, durations 51–800 ms, only the proxy's ingress/egress spans affected, no frontend error span, backend pod ready with 0 restarts). It is not proven: the frontend server's keep-alive/timeout settings and the Envoy cluster upstream idle-timeout/health-check configuration could not be read.

A second candidate contributor is frontend runtime/resource pressure: the container is throttled in 34.5% of CFS periods under a 100m CPU limit and its V8 old_space sits at 35–45 MB of a ~51 MB limit, so GC/CPU stalls could occasionally prevent the frontend from serving an accepted connection. Not proven as the cause: UC denotes a connection termination rather than a response timeout, average CPU use was only ~52% of the limit, memory was 128 MiB of 200Mi, and no frontend ERROR spans or restarts appear.

Rejected: a frontend pod crash, OOM kill or rollout as the cause of the 503s. The frontend pod is the same instance created at 12:12:01Z with restart count 0, Running/ready, its deployment reports 1/1 available and ready, and no old-space exhaustion or container memory approach to the 200Mi limit is visible (128 MiB at 13:05).

Rejected: frontend-proxy's own resource exhaustion or upstream-overflow behaviour as the cause. Its container used ~0.014 of a 0.03-core limit and ~20.2 MB of 50Mi, was throttled in only 7.0% of CFS periods, and the logged failures carry the UC / upstream_reset_before_response_started{connection_termination} signature naming the frontend endpoint rather than a proxy-side overflow or no-healthy-upstream condition.

Rejected: the frontend returning application-level 5xx responses. The frontend's span metrics show 0 STATUS_CODE_ERROR on every operation, and in the sampled failing traces the proxy's egress span has http.status_code="0" (no response received) and the failed request has no frontend server span, so no frontend response was produced for these requests.

The error spans seen in ad, fraud-detection and recommendation do not tie to this alert's mechanism: they are all on flagd event-stream operations (flagd.evaluation.v1.Service/EventStream for ad and fraud-detection, /flagd.evaluation.v1.Service/EventStream for recommendation), whereas the alerting failures are frontend-proxy ingress spans to the frontend upstream; no evidence links those flagd stream errors to frontend-proxy's 503s.

gaps: The alert rule RequestErrorRate is not loaded in the queried Prometheus (list_prometheus_rules with rule_name=RequestErrorRate returned no data), so the alert expression and the annotation's 'current: 0.01111111111111111' could not be reproduced; the largest frontend-proxy error fraction computable here is 0.00116 of frontend-proxy spans per 10 minutes on the "ingress" operation.

Frontend application logs could not be read: fetch_pod_logs for frontend-675fd7b5c5-ssc7t returned 0 lines / 0 bytes (status no_data, no previous container instance), so the frontend's application-level reason for terminating upstream connections is unverified.

The frontend-proxy access-log read stopped at the 4 MiB limit reading through 2026-11-15T12:45:25.87Z, so 503 UC log lines after that time are unknown even though span metrics show frontend-proxy errors continuing to 13:06:59.
Jaeger trace data for the frontend-proxy sample ends at 2026-11-15T12:45:09.10Z, so trace-level error detail after 12:45 is unknown (the last sampled 503 is at 12:45:08.712).

No frontend-proxy Envoy configuration is exposed in the cluster (no Envoy ConfigMap exists in otel-demo; configuration is baked into the image), so upstream connection-pool idle timeout, health-check and retry settings cannot be inspected to confirm or refute the keep-alive/connection-drain hypotheses.

Kubernetes events could not be used: a non-Normal event query for otel-demo returned no data (its window covered only 12:48:58–13:00:58), so absence of eviction, OOM or probe-failure events during the incident is unverified.
Runtime flag state during the incident is unknown (no change_history integration); only the flagd ConfigMap defaults read at 13:10:22 were observable, and all fault flags were "off" in that file.

No pre-incident baseline exists in the available data (metric series start ~12:26:59 and the demo pods started ~12:12), so no latency trend and no change point for the connection-termination rate can be established.
next_steps: Compare the frontend's Node/Next.js server keep-alive/headers timeout settings with the Envoy upstream cluster idle timeout for the frontend cluster, and lengthen the frontend keep-alive timeout or disable upstream connection reuse races if a keep-alive close race is confirmed.

Restore/read frontend stdout logging (or check node/kubelet logs) around 12:26:16, 12:33:04, 12:34:00, 12:34:43, 12:40:52, 12:44:20 and 12:45:08 to see whether the frontend logged socket closures or event-loop stalls at those instants.

Correlate each 503 UC line with the preceding request on the same upstream ephemeral port in the full Envoy access log to distinguish idle-connection close from connection draining on health-check transitions.

Review whether the frontend's 100m CPU limit (34.5% of CFS periods throttled, ~0.052 cores used) and ~51 MB V8 old_space are appropriate for the load-generator's ~12 req/s, and raise the limit only if further evidence ties throttling to the connection terminations.
